newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso wins key vote on re-election.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso wins key vote on re-election.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Tuesday won a key battle in his plan to become Brazil's first re-elected leader when the lower house of Congress approved a bill allowing him to run again.

Chamber of Deputy officials said 336 deputies voted in favour of changing the constitution to allow sitting presidents, governors and mayors to seek a second consecutive term. Only 308 votes, or 60 percent of the house, were needed.
"The bill is approved," said lower house President Luiz Eduardo Magalhaes as government supporters broke into a round of cheers and backslapping.
Through his spokesman, Sergio Amaral, Cardoso thanked Congress for the "serene" manner in which it voted.
"He sees it as a decision to carry on the policy of economic stability ... and a disposition to continue on the path of transformation of Brazilian society," Amaral told reporters.

Brazil has banned re-election since the founding of the republic in 1889 because of fears of a revival of past imperial powers. But Cardoso argues the economic reforms he launched as finance minister in 1994 need political continuity to prosper.

The bill must be approved again by the lower house and then twice by the Senate. If it passes, Cardoso would join presidents Carlos Menem of Argentina and Alberto Fujimori of Peru as Latin American leaders who have rewritten their countries' constitutions to allow their own re-elections.

The first vote in the chamber was regarded as the crucial test. As late as last Friday, the passage of the bill was in doubt because of a rebellion by some factions in the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), Congress' largest party and a nominal Cardoso ally.

This week government whips said they had overcome resistance. Nevertheless, they flew in sick deputies and Political Affairs Minister Luis Carlos Santos stepped down from his post on Tuesday morning to be able to vote as a deputy.
"This is a historic decision. Brazil has assured the continuity of modernisation," Santos said after the vote.
Opponents from left and right-wing parties, who accused Cardoso of seeking to further his own political power, buried ideological differences to find ways of obstructing the bill.
They can still hamper its progress by proposing amendments on Wednesday.
Some amendments that must still be voted on include a proposal to tie re-election to a plebiscite or force the office holder to step down six months before an election.

Analysts say the prospect of four more years on top of the two left in his current term would bolster Cardoso's support in Brazil's notoriously volatile Congress. He would then find it easier to push through reforms to streamline the state, which have been paralysed for months amid re-election fever.
But if he loses, Cardoso may be unable to maintain control over his unruly allies in the run-up to the 1998 elections, the analysts say.
